title: A rigged coin, 50 flips: caught?
hook: The coin really is rigged toward heads. Will a standard 5% test on 50 flips spot it?

knows: a test at the 5% level rarely flags a fair coin (p-values)
doesNotKnow: that a real effect can be missed most of the time
that more flips raise the chance of catching it

misconception: If a real effect exists, a standard 5% test will find it.
objective: The learner can say that a 5% test only controls false alarms; with few flips it misses a real 60% bias about two times in three, and more flips raise the catch rate.
keyState: 100 seeded 50-flip experiments run (28 of 100 reach the bar of 32), then the same 100 experiments extended to 200 flips (80 of 100 reach the bar of 113).

claims.text: The coin is secretly 60% heads; each experiment flips it 50 times and calls it biased only if heads reaches 32 or more.
claims.source: Set-up shown on the stage. 32 is the smallest c with P(Bin(50, 0.5) >= c) <= 0.05 (bar(50) in model.ts).

claims.text: A fair coin reaches 32 heads in 50 flips 3.2% of the time.
claims.source: P(Bin(50, 0.5) >= 32) = 0.03245 (exact binomial sum; falseAlarm(50), recomputed in node). P(>= 31) is 0.0595, which is why the bar is 32.

claims.text: A 60% coin reaches 32 heads in 50 flips about 34% of the time, so the test catches the bias about one time in three.
In the 100 experiments on the stage, 28 of 100 reached the bar of 32 heads with 50 flips.
claims.source: Seeds mulberry32(7000 + i), i = 0..99, 60% heads per flip; 7000 was the first seed tried (untuned). Over 400 other sets of 100 experiments the count averaged 33.2 with SD 4.7 (range 20 to 47), so 28 is a typical-low draw, not the rule; the exact rate is 33.6%.

claims.text: With 200 flips and a bar of 113 heads, a fair coin reaches the bar 3.8% of the time and the 60% coin reaches it 86.0% of the time.
claims.source: bar(200) = 113 is the smallest c with P(Bin(200, 0.5) >= c) <= 0.05; P(Bin(200, 0.5) >= 113) = 0.0384; P(Bin(200, 0.6) >= 113) = 0.8603 (exact; power(200), recomputed in node).

claims.text: In the same 100 experiments extended to 200 flips, 80 of 100 reached the bar of 113 heads.
claims.source: Same seeds, first 50 flips of each stream unchanged. Over 400 other sets the count averaged 85.8 with SD 3.5 (range 74 to 95); the exact rate is 86.0%.

claims.text: Not finding a significant result from a small test does not show there is no effect.
claims.source: Standard interpretation of statistical power: with a 34% catch rate, a null result is the usual outcome even though the effect is real (claims 3 and 4).

recall.question: A drug truly works, but a small trial finds 'no significant effect'. What is the sensible reading?
options: The trial may simply have been too small to catch a real effect
recall.why: A small test misses a real effect most of the time (a 60% coin in 50 flips is caught only about a third of the time). More data raises the catch rate.
